steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Hardwoods: broad-leaved deciduous trees - dense, strong, durable, slow-growing (30-100 years). Oak (furniture, flooring), mahogany (boat building), ash (tool handles, sports equipment).

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Softwoods: coniferous evergreen trees - less dense, faster growing (10-30 years), easier to work. Pine (construction, furniture), cedar (outdoor, rot-resistant), spruce (structural, instruments).

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Plywood: thin veneers glued with grain alternating at 90 degrees - prevents warping, strong in all directions.

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: MDF: wood fibres bonded with resin - smooth, uniform, no grain direction, takes paint well, but dust is hazardous when cutting.

steps.title: Try it yourself
steps.body: Explain why plywood is less likely to warp than solid timber of the same thickness. | A designer is making a kitchen worktop. Compare solid oak and MDF, justifying your recommendation. | Discuss the environmental advantages and disadvantages of using hardwoods in product design.

steps.title: Check your answers
steps.body: Solid timber has grain in one direction - it warps along the grain as moisture changes. Plywood's alternating veneer layers create opposing grain directions that cancel out warping forces. | Solid oak: beautiful grain, very durable, water-resistant with treatment - but expensive, can warp, heavy. MDF: smooth, uniform, does not warp, affordable - but swells if water penetrates, cannot be r | Advantages: durable (products last decades), repairable, biodegradable, carbon-neutral if sustainably sourced. Disadvantages: slow growth, deforestation risk, high transport miles, illegal logging con

steps.title: Exam tips
steps.body: Hardwood/softwood is about tree type, NOT wood hardness (balsa is a hardwood but very soft) Always mention FSC certification when discussing timber sustainability MDF dust is a specific health hazard - examiners test this
